blocks.text: A commercial bakery's gas oven burns the same fuel every day but its flue analyser swings between 2 % and 8 % oxygen as the damper drifts. At 2 % the flame is hot and efficient; at 8 % almost a third more fuel is needed for the same bake. The key to reading that analyser, and to predicting how hot the flame can get, is the stoichiometry of the reaction.

blocks.markdown: **Stoichiometric combustion** is the reaction in which a fuel burns completely with exactly the oxygen it needs: all carbon becomes CO$_2$, all hydrogen becomes H$_2$O, and no oxygen is left over. We balance atoms on a kilomole basis. Air is treated as 21 % O$_2$ and 79 % N$_2$ by volume, so each kmol of O$_2$ comes with 3.76 kmol of N$_2$ (79/21), giving 4.76 kmol of air per kmol of O$_2$. Nitrogen is inert in this model.

blocks.caption: $a$ is the kmol of O$_2$ required per kmol of fuel

blocks.title: Air-fuel ratio
blocks.text: The mass air-fuel ratio is $AFR=\dfrac{m_{air}}{m_{fuel}}=\dfrac{4.76\,a\,M_{air}}{M_{fuel}}$ with $M_{air}=28.97$ kg/kmol. Excess air $e$ is the fraction of air supplied beyond the stoichiometric amount; the actual air is $(1+e)$ times the stoichiometric air.

blocks.title: Stoichiometric air-fuel ratio for propane
blocks.prompt: Balance the combustion of propane ($\mathrm{C_3H_8}$, molar mass 44.10 kg/kmol) in air and find the stoichiometric air requirement per kmol and per kg of fuel.

steps.text: Atoms: C gives 3 CO$_2$, H gives 4 H$_2$O; count oxygen atoms on the right.

blocks.answer: Propane needs 23.8 kmol of air per kmol of fuel, an air-fuel ratio of 15.6 kg/kg.

blocks.markdown: Real burners supply more air than the stoichiometric amount to make sure all fuel is burned. If a fraction $e$ of excess air is supplied, the products also contain the unused oxygen $ae$ and extra nitrogen. Flue gas analysers cool the sample and remove water, so they report a **dry** volume (mole) fraction, which excludes H$_2$O. For complete combustion the dry products per kmol of fuel are $x$ of CO$_2$, $ae$ of O$_2$, and $3.76a(1+e)$ of N$_2$. The measured dry oxygen fraction therefore determines $e$.

blocks.caption: Complete combustion; $y_{O_2}$ is the dry O$_2$ mole fraction; for a quick estimate $e\approx y_{O_2}/(0.21-y_{O_2})$

blocks.title: Excess air from a dry flue measurement
blocks.prompt: A propane burner has a dry flue gas oxygen reading of 4.0 %. Assuming complete combustion, find the excess air.

steps.text: Check by recomputing the oxygen fraction.

blocks.answer: The excess air is 21.5 %. The quick formula $0.04/(0.21-0.04)=23.5$ % gives a slightly different value because it neglects the CO$_2$ and the fuel.

blocks.title: More air is not free
blocks.text: Excess air ensures complete combustion, but every extra kmol of air carries inert nitrogen and surplus oxygen that must be heated to the flue temperature, which wastes heat and lowers the flame temperature. A burner is tuned for the smallest excess air that still burns the fuel cleanly.

blocks.markdown: The **adiabatic flame temperature** $T_{ad}$ is the temperature the products would reach if no heat were lost to the surroundings and no work done, for complete combustion at constant pressure. The enthalpy balance says that the reactants' enthalpy equals the products' enthalpy. With reactants at $T_0=298$ K, this is the same as saying that the heating value of the fuel raises the products from 298 K to $T_{ad}$. Taking mean molar specific heats $\bar c_{p,i}$ over the range, and using the lower heating value (LHV) because the water leaves as vapour, the balance becomes simple.

blocks.caption: LHV in kJ/kmol of fuel; $n_i$ kmol of product $i$ per kmol of fuel; mean $\bar c_p$ in kJ/kmol K
Assumed mean specific heats (typical): CO$_2$ 55, H$_2$O 43, N$_2$ 33, O$_2$ 35 kJ/kmol K; methane LHV 802.3 MJ/kmol.

blocks.title: Adiabatic flame temperature of methane
blocks.prompt: Methane burns with stoichiometric air at 298 K. Use LHV = 802.3 MJ/kmol and the mean specific heats in the table caption. Estimate $T_{ad}$.
blocks.answer: $T_{ad}\approx2360$ K. Measured values are lower (about 2200 K) because dissociation of CO$_2$ and H$_2$O absorbs energy and the mean specific heats are approximate. With 20 % excess air the estimate falls to about 2070 K.

blocks.title: Dry versus wet
blocks.text: Flue gas analysers report on a dry basis. Using a wet basis, or forgetting that water has been removed, will give a wrong excess air. Also, the formula above assumes no CO or unburned fuel; with CO in the flue gas, the oxygen fraction no longer maps simply to excess air.

points: Stoichiometric air for $\mathrm{C_xH_y}$ is $a=x+y/4$ kmol of O$_2$, with 4.76 kmol of air per kmol of O$_2$; $AFR=4.76aM_{air}/M_{fuel}$.
Excess air follows from the dry O$_2$ fraction: $y_{O_2}=ae/[x+ae+3.76a(1+e)]$.
Adiabatic flame temperature comes from $LHV=\sum n_i\bar c_{p,i}(T_{ad}-T_0)$ and is reduced by excess air.
Real flame temperatures are below the ideal estimate because of dissociation and heat loss.

questions.stem: Butane (C4H10, molar mass 58.12 kg/kmol) burns completely with stoichiometric air (21 percent O2, 79 percent N2 by volume, molar mass of air 28.97 kg/kmol). Find the mass air-fuel ratio in kg of air per kg of fuel.
questions.explanation: The oxygen required is a = 4 + 10/4 = 6.5 kmol per kmol fuel, so the air is 6.5 x 4.76 = 30.94 kmol. The mass ratio is 30.94 x 28.97/58.12 = 15.42 kg/kg.

questions.stem: Methanol (CH3OH, molar mass 32.04 kg/kmol) burns completely with stoichiometric air to give CO2 and H2O. What is the mass air-fuel ratio (molar mass of air 28.97 kg/kmol)?

options.text: About 17.19 kg air per kg fuel
About 8.61 kg air per kg fuel
About 6.46 kg air per kg fuel
About 1.36 kg air per kg fuel

questions.correctOptionText: About 6.46 kg air per kg fuel

distractorRationale.a: That is the ratio for methane (CH4); methanol contains oxygen in the fuel, which reduces the air needed.
distractorRationale.b: This uses a = x + y/4 = 2 and ignores the oxygen in the fuel, which supplies half a kmol of O2.
distractorRationale.d: This uses kmol of oxygen instead of kmol of air; air is 4.76 kmol per kmol O2.

questions.explanation: Balancing gives CH3OH + 1.5 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O, so the air is 1.5 x 4.76 = 7.14 kmol per kmol fuel. The mass ratio is 7.14 x 28.97/32.04 = 6.46, much less than for hydrocarbons because the fuel already contains oxygen.

questions.stem: A burner fires ethane (C2H6) and the dry flue gas contains 5.0 percent O2 by volume. Assuming complete combustion, find the excess air as a percentage of the stoichiometric air.
questions.explanation: For ethane x = 2 and a = 3.5. Then e = y(x + 3.76a)/(a - 4.76 a y) = 0.05 x 15.16/(3.5 - 0.833) = 0.758/2.667 = 0.2842, i.e. 28.4 %. The quick formula 5/(21-5) would give 31 percent, so the exact form matters at high oxygen.

questions.stem: Methane burns with 30 percent excess air. Assuming complete combustion, find the dry-basis oxygen content of the flue gas in percent by volume.
questions.explanation: Per kmol of methane, a = 2 so excess O2 = 2 x 0.3 = 0.6 kmol. Dry products: CO2 1, O2 0.6 and N2 3.76 x 2 x 1.3 = 9.776, total 11.376 kmol, so y(O2) = 0.6/11.376 = 5.27 %. Water is excluded because the sample is dried.

questions.stem: Hydrogen burns with stoichiometric air at 298 K: H2 + 0.5 (O2 + 3.76 N2) gives H2O (vapour) + 1.88 N2. Use LHV = 241.8 MJ/kmol of H2 and mean specific heats of 42 kJ/kmol K for H2O and 32.5 kJ/kmol K for N2. Estimate the adiabatic flame temperature in K, neglecting dissociation.
questions.explanation: The product heat capacity is 42 + 1.88 x 32.5 = 103.1 kJ/K per kmol H2. The temperature rise is 241 800/103.1 = 2345 K, so T = 298 + 2345 = 2643 K. Dissociation would lower the true value by a few hundred kelvin.

questions.stem: A furnace operator increases the excess air from 10 % to 40 % at the same fuel rate. What is the effect on the adiabatic flame temperature?

options.text: It decreases, because the extra nitrogen and oxygen must be heated by the same fuel energy
It increases, because more oxygen gives a more complete reaction
It is unchanged, because the fuel energy is the same
It increases, because the air enters at a high temperature

questions.correctOptionText: It decreases, because the extra nitrogen and oxygen must be heated by the same fuel energy

distractorRationale.b: The reaction was already complete; the extra air only dilutes the products.
distractorRationale.c: The same energy heats more product mass, so the temperature rise is smaller.
distractorRationale.d: Air enters at ambient temperature, so it acts as a heat sink, not a heat source.

questions.explanation: In the balance $LHV=\sum n_i\bar c_{p,i}\Delta T$ the right-hand sum grows with excess air, so $\Delta T$ falls for the same LHV. The stoichiometric mixture gives the highest ideal flame temperature.

questions.stem: Why are measured flame temperatures lower than the adiabatic flame temperature calculated for complete combustion with constant specific heats?

options.text: Dissociation of CO2 and H2O absorbs energy, and heat is lost by radiation and conduction from the real flame
The adiabatic temperature calculation includes losses that real flames avoid
Real flames burn more fuel than the calculation assumes
The specific heat of the products rises to zero at high temperature

questions.correctOptionText: Dissociation of CO2 and H2O absorbs energy, and heat is lost by radiation and conduction from the real flame

distractorRationale.b: The adiabatic calculation assumes no heat loss, so it overestimates.
distractorRationale.c: The calculation uses the same fuel energy; additional fuel is not a typical difference.
distractorRationale.d: Specific heats rise with temperature; this lowers the temperature rise, but the main differences are dissociation and heat loss.

questions.explanation: At flame temperatures above about 1800 K, CO2 and H2O partly dissociate, an endothermic process that takes energy from the products. Heat loss through radiation adds to the shortfall, so the real temperature is below the ideal estimate.

questions.stem: A burner runs at 25 percent excess air. What is the equivalence ratio (actual fuel-air ratio divided by the stoichiometric fuel-air ratio)?

options.text: 0.25, because the equivalence ratio equals the excess air fraction

distractorRationale.b: That is the air ratio ($\lambda$), the inverse of the equivalence ratio.
distractorRationale.c: The excess air fraction is not the equivalence ratio.
distractorRationale.d: A burner with excess air is fuel-lean, with an equivalence ratio below one.

questions.explanation: Excess air means more air than needed, so the fuel-air ratio is lower than stoichiometric: $\phi=1/(1+e)=0.80$. Lean mixtures (below one) have lower flame temperatures than the stoichiometric case.

questions.stem: Describe the steps to find the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio for a hydrocarbon $\mathrm{C_xH_y}$ and explain why the nitrogen in the air is included even though it does not react.
markingGuide: Balance C to give $x$ CO$_2$ and H to give $y/2$ H$_2$O; count oxygen atoms to find $a=x+y/4$
Write air as O$_2$ + 3.76 N$_2$, so air per kmol O$_2$ is 4.76 kmol
Nitrogen is inert but carried through, appearing in the products as $3.76a$ kmol
Nitrogen must be included because it affects the mass of air required, the product composition and the heat capacity of the products (flame temperature)
questions.explanation: The balance fixes the oxygen needed, and the air mass follows from the 79:21 N2:O2 ratio. Nitrogen does not burn but it dominates the flue gas and absorbs heat, so it must be included in composition and flame temperature calculations.

questions.stem: Explain how a dry flue gas oxygen measurement is used to determine excess air, and discuss two reasons why the same measurement would give a misleading result if the combustion were incomplete or the sample were wet.
markingGuide: Analyser measures O$_2$ in dry products, $y_{O_2}=ae/[x+ae+3.76a(1+e)]$, which can be solved for $e$
Recognises the approximation $e\approx y/(0.21-y)$ and its limits
If combustion is incomplete, CO and unburned hydrocarbons consume or leave oxygen so the O$_2$ reading under-represents the air supplied, and the formula must be modified
If a wet sample were used, the mole fractions would include H$_2$O, changing the denominator and the apparent oxygen fraction
Air leakage into the flue or sample line adds oxygen that is not from the burner, inflating the apparent excess air
questions.explanation: The oxygen left over after complete combustion measures how much more air was supplied than needed. Incomplete combustion, water in the sample or leaks all alter the oxygen balance and distort the result, so the reading must be interpreted together with CO and sample conditions.
